en: Extremely miserable or hopeless; completely without pride or dignity
hook: AB-JECT: thrown (ject) away (ab), cast down to the lowest point.
story: Abject. After the cyclone, Nasima's family lost their house, their boat, and their two cows in a single night. For weeks they slept under a plastic sheet beside the embankment, with no money and nothing to eat but relief rice. They lived in abject poverty: extremely miserable and hopeless. Abject can also describe behaviour completely without pride, as in an abject apology. Think: ab means away, and ject means thrown, so abject means cast down. Synonyms: wretched, hopeless, servile.

gre.s: Far from the defiant statement his supporters expected, the senator issued an ____ apology, begging forgiveness and conceding every one of his critics' points.
gre.clue: begging forgiveness and conceding every one of his critics' points

en: Friendly and without serious disagreement
hook: AMICABLE: AMIGO (friend) + able.
story: Amicable. After ten years as business partners, Farzana and Tamim decided to go their separate ways. There was no shouting, no lawyers, no lawsuits. They divided the clients fairly, shook hands, and still meet for tea every month. Their separation was amicable: friendly and without serious disagreement. Amicable comes from Latin amicus, friend, like amigo in Spanish. Amiable describes a pleasant person; amicable describes relations and agreements. Synonyms: cordial, harmonious, peaceable. Opposite: hostile.

gre.s: Although the negotiations had been tense, the two companies reached an ____ settlement, parting on such good terms that they later launched a joint venture.
gre.clue: parting on such good terms that they later launched a joint venture

en: Strong hostility or hatred
hook: ANIMOSITY: like ANIMALS growling at each other.
story: Animosity. Two neighbouring families in a village near Bogura have not spoken for twenty years. It began with a quarrel over one metre of land along a boundary. Since then, they have skipped each other's weddings, refused to share a well, and even taught their children to glare across the lane. The animosity between them is fierce: strong hostility or hatred. Think of its cousin animus, which also means hostile feeling. Synonyms: enmity, antagonism, rancour. Opposite: goodwill.

gre.s: The two former allies now regard each other with open ____, refusing even to appear on the same stage after their bitter public quarrel.
gre.clue: after their bitter public quarrel

en: To state or assert something to be true, firmly
hook: AVER: 'A-VERity', declaring the truth.
story: Aver. In the courtroom, the lawyer asked the witness whether she was certain. She looked straight at the judge. "I saw him with my own eyes. He was there at ten o'clock. I am completely sure." She averred it: she stated firmly that it was true. Aver is a formal word, common in law and argument. It comes from Latin verus, true, as in verify and verity: to aver is to declare something true. Synonyms: assert, affirm, maintain. Opposite: deny.

gre.s: Even under intense cross-examination, the witness continued to ____ that she had seen the defendant at the scene, never once wavering from her account.
gre.clue: never once wavering from her account

en: An overwhelming outpouring of many things at once
hook: BARRAGE: like a BARRAGE of artillery fire.
story: Barrage. The moment the actor stepped out of the airport, dozens of journalists rushed toward her. Cameras flashed, microphones were pushed at her face, and questions came from every direction at once. She faced a barrage of questions: an overwhelming outpouring of many things at once. Originally, a barrage was heavy, continuous artillery fire. It can also mean a dam built across a river, like the Farakka Barrage. Synonyms: onslaught, deluge, torrent, volley. Opposite: trickle.

gre.s: Upon announcing the controversial policy, the minister faced a ____ of criticism so relentless that she withdrew the proposal within a week.
gre.clue: so relentless that she withdrew the proposal within a week

en: Providing emotional release and relief
hook: CATHARTIC: a CAT-HEART cleanse — releases what's trapped inside.
story: Cathartic. For months, Lima kept her grief for her grandmother bottled up. She went to classes, smiled, and told everyone she was fine. Then one evening she sat with an old photo album and cried for an hour. Afterward she felt lighter than she had in months. The crying was cathartic: it provided emotional release and relief. Catharsis is Greek for cleansing or purging, and Aristotle said tragedy is cathartic for its audience. Synonyms: purging, cleansing, liberating.

gre.s: Many survivors found testifying in public unexpectedly ____: after years of silence, describing what they had endured at last brought them a sense of release.
gre.clue: at last brought them a sense of release

en: To figure out the meaning of something hard to read or understand
hook: DE-CIPHER: undo the CIPHER (code).
story: Decipher. Rafsan found his grandfather's letters from the nineteen fifties in a tin trunk. They were written in faded ink, in tiny cursive Bangla, with half the words smudged by rain. He spent a whole weekend with a magnifying glass, comparing letters and guessing words from context, until the sentences finally made sense. He had deciphered them: figured out the meaning of something hard to read or understand. A cipher is a secret code. Synonyms: decode, interpret, unravel.

gre.s: The doctor's handwriting was so illegible that even the experienced pharmacist could not ____ the prescription without calling the clinic for help.
gre.clue: handwriting was so illegible

en: A false belief held firmly despite evidence against it
hook: DELUSION: an ILLUSION you won't let go of.
story: Delusion. Tareq failed his practice tests month after month, never opened his vocabulary list, and skipped every mock exam. Yet he told everyone he would score in the top one percent because he was naturally smart. His friends warned him; he laughed. He was living under a delusion: a false belief held firmly despite evidence against it. Delusions of grandeur are fantasies about one's own greatness. Compare illusion, a false perception of the senses. Synonyms: fantasy, misconception, self-deception.

gre.s: Despite mounting evidence that his company was bankrupt, the founder clung to the ____ that a single blockbuster product would restore its fortunes.
gre.clue: Despite mounting evidence that his company was bankrupt

en: To distribute; to provide (a service)
hook: DISPENSE: like a water DISPENSER giving out water.
story: Dispense. At the clinic on a remote char island, the only nurse, Shefali Apa, sits behind a wooden table every morning. She checks blood pressure, cleans wounds, and dispenses medicines from a metal cabinet to a long line of patients. To dispense is to distribute or provide. Pharmacists dispense prescriptions, machines dispense tickets, and judges dispense justice. Watch for dispense with, which means to do without: let us dispense with formalities. Synonyms: distribute, allocate, administer. Opposite: withhold.

gre.s: Rather than stockpile the scarce grain, the village council chose to ____ it equally among all households, giving each family the same small ration.
gre.clue: giving each family the same small ration

en: Fluent, persuasive, and expressive in speaking or writing
hook: E-LOQU-ENT: 'loqu' means speak. Speaks beautifully.
story: Eloquent. At the inter-college debate, a shy first-year student from a village school spoke last. She talked for only three minutes, about her mother, who sold vegetables on the roadside to pay for her books. Her words were simple, but so moving that the judges stopped writing and the hall fell silent. She was eloquent: fluent, persuasive, and expressive. Eloquent comes from Latin loqui, to speak, as in loquacious. Even a silence can be eloquent. Synonyms: articulate, expressive, persuasive.

gre.s: Though the senator was famously awkward in live debates, his written speeches were remarkably ____, moving even his opponents with their clarity and grace.
gre.clue: moving even his opponents with their clarity and grace

en: To capture someone's complete attention; to fascinate
hook: ENTHRALL: like a THRALL (slave) to the story.
story: Enthrall. Every evening, Grandfather Moti sits on the veranda and tells ghost stories about the old banyan tree. All the children of the neighbourhood gather at his feet. Nobody fidgets, nobody checks a phone; even the cat seems to listen. He enthralls them: he captures their complete attention and fascinates them. A thrall was once a slave, so an enthralled audience is held captive by wonder. Synonyms: captivate, spellbind, mesmerize, rivet. Opposite: bore.

gre.s: Her storytelling could ____ even the most restless audience: children who usually fidgeted through lessons sat motionless until the final word.
gre.clue: children who usually fidgeted through lessons sat motionless until the final word

en: To destroy or get rid of completely
hook: E-RADIC-ATE: pull out by the ROOTS (radix).
story: Eradicate. In the early nineteen seventies, Bangladesh was one of the last places on earth with smallpox. Health workers went village by village, vaccinating people and tracking every case. In 1975, a little girl from Bhola named Rahima Banu became the last person in the world to catch the deadliest natural form of the disease. Soon smallpox was eradicated: destroyed completely. Eradicate comes from e, out, plus radix, root: pulled out by the roots. Synonyms: eliminate, extirpate, wipe out.

gre.s: Public health officials hoped not merely to control the disease but to ____ it entirely, so that no new cases would ever appear again.
gre.clue: so that no new cases would ever appear again

en: New and inexperienced; a young bird just learning to fly
hook: FLEDGLING: a baby bird just getting its feathers.
story: Fledgling. Each spring, a pair of mynas nests under the roof of Rupa's house. One morning she saw a fledgling on the windowsill: a young bird, newly feathered, flapping its wings but too scared to leap. Three days later, it flew to the guava tree. As an adjective, fledgling means new and inexperienced: a fledgling business, a fledgling democracy. A fledgling has only just fledged, or grown its flying feathers. Synonyms: budding, novice, nascent. Opposite: veteran.

gre.s: Like many ____ enterprises, the start-up struggled during its first year, lacking both the experience and the capital that established competitors enjoyed.
gre.clue: lacking both the experience and the capital that established competitors enjoyed

en: Courage and strength of mind in facing pain or adversity
hook: FORTITUDE: a FORT inside your mind.
story: Fortitude. Mina was nineteen when her father was paralysed in a road accident. She took a job at a pharmacy, nursed him every evening, and still finished her degree, studying at night beside his bed. She never complained, though she was often exhausted. Her neighbours admired her fortitude: courage and strength of mind in facing pain or adversity. Fortitude comes from Latin fortis, strong, as in fort and fortify. Synonyms: resilience, grit, endurance, backbone. Opposite: faintheartedness.

gre.s: The patient endured months of painful treatment with remarkable ____, never complaining even when the doctors warned that recovery might take years.
gre.clue: never complaining even when the doctors warned

en: Happening by chance, especially lucky chance
hook: FORTUITOUS: FORTUNE-ate by chance.
story: Fortuitous. Shakil missed his bus to Chattogram and had to wait two hours for the next one. On that later bus, he happened to sit beside the managing director of a company he had applied to. They talked the whole journey, and a week later he had the job. The meeting was fortuitous: happening by chance, especially lucky chance. Strictly, fortuitous means unplanned, while fortunate simply means lucky. The best fortuitous events are both. Synonyms: accidental, serendipitous. Opposite: planned.

gre.s: The discovery of penicillin was largely ____: Fleming noticed the mold only because he had left a dish of bacteria unwashed before going on holiday.
gre.clue: only because he had left a dish of bacteria unwashed

en: To provoke or urge someone into action
hook: GOAD: a pointed stick used to push cattle forward.
story: Goad. In the fields near Jashore, a farmer walks behind his two oxen with a long pointed stick, prodding them whenever they slow down. That stick is a goad. Today the word is mostly figurative. When Zara's friends kept teasing that she was too scared to apply to Harvard, they goaded her into it, and she applied the next day. To goad is to provoke or urge someone into action. Synonyms: spur, prod, provoke, incite. Opposite: deter.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the prime minister into calling an early election, the opposition filled parliament with taunts, but she refused to be provoked.
gre.clue: the opposition filled parliament with taunts

en: About to happen
hook: IMMINENT: IN a MINute it will happen.
story: Imminent. The radio crackled: a cyclone was two hundred kilometres away and would strike the Khulna coast within hours. In a coastal village, volunteers ran from house to house with megaphones, and families hurried toward the concrete shelter. Danger was imminent: about to happen. Do not confuse imminent with eminent, which means famous and respected. Imminent things loom over you, like the dark cyclone clouds. Synonyms: impending, looming, approaching. Opposites: distant, remote.

gre.s: Although officials insisted there was no cause for alarm, residents could see that the dam's collapse was ____, as water was already spilling over its cracked walls.
gre.clue: water was already spilling over its cracked walls

en: Impossible to deny or dispute
hook: IN-CONTROVERT-IBLE: NO CONTROVERSY possible.
story: Incontrovertible. For a year, the factory owner denied dumping chemicals into the river. Then a student journalist hid a camera on the bank. The footage showed the factory's pipe pouring black waste straight into the water, with a clear timestamp, and lab tests matched the chemicals. The evidence was incontrovertible: impossible to deny or dispute. Break it down: in means not, and controvert means to argue against, as in controversy. Synonyms: indisputable, irrefutable, undeniable. Opposite: questionable.

gre.s: Although the theory was once fiercely contested, the satellite data now provide ____ proof, leaving even the most skeptical scientists with no grounds for doubt.
gre.clue: leaving even the most skeptical scientists with no grounds for doubt

en: Traveling from place to place
hook: ITINERANT: always following an ITINERARY.
story: Itinerant. Long ago, a bioscope man would arrive in Tapan's grandfather's village every few weeks, carrying a painted wooden box on his back. Children paid a few coins to peer at its pictures. He slept on a kind family's veranda, then moved on to the next village. He was itinerant: travelling from place to place. Itinerant shares a root with itinerary, a travel plan. Itinerant preachers, musicians, and workers. Synonyms: wandering, roving, nomadic, peripatetic. Opposite: settled.

gre.s: Unlike his ancestors, who had farmed the same land for centuries, the musician led an ____ life, performing in a different town almost every night.
gre.clue: performing in a different town almost every night

en: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or weaker person
hook: MAGNA-NIMOUS: a MAGNIFICENT spirit (animus).
story: Magnanimous. Sadia's team won the debate final against bitter rivals who had mocked them all season. Instead of gloating, Sadia praised the losing captain's argument in front of the whole hall. Months later, when he was preparing for a national contest, she helped him practise. She was magnanimous: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone weaker. Magna means great and animus means spirit, so magnanimous means great-souled. Synonyms: big-hearted, gracious, noble. Opposite: petty, vindictive.

gre.s: In victory, the general proved ____, pardoning the defeated soldiers and allowing them to return home rather than seeking revenge.
gre.clue: pardoning the defeated soldiers

en: Deserving praise or reward
hook: MERITORIOUS: full of MERIT.
story: Meritorious. During a flood, a young police constable in Sirajganj waded through chest-deep water for two days, carrying old people and children to safety. He rescued more than sixty villagers. Later he received a medal for meritorious service: deserving praise or reward. Meritorious comes from merit, the quality of deserving. Top students win merit scholarships. Meritorious means more than merely good; it means good enough to earn recognition. Synonyms: praiseworthy, commendable, laudable. Opposite: blameworthy.

gre.s: The committee rejected his nomination, arguing that his work, while competent, was not especially ____ and did nothing to distinguish him from his peers.
gre.clue: did nothing to distinguish him from his peers

en: An open rebellion against authority, especially by soldiers or sailors
hook: MUTINY: the crew MUTES the captain and takes over.
story: Mutiny. On a cargo ship in the Bay of Bengal, the crew had not been paid for four months, and the captain had locked away the food stores. One morning, the sailors refused to work, took over the bridge, and locked the captain in his cabin until the owners promised their wages. It was a mutiny: an open rebellion against authority, especially by soldiers or sailors. The most famous may be the mutiny on the Bounty in 1789. Synonyms: revolt, insurrection, uprising.

gre.s: Exhausted by months of harsh discipline and dwindling rations, the sailors threatened to ____ unless the captain agreed to turn the ship toward home.
gre.clue: unless the captain agreed to turn the ship toward home

en: Seemingly contradictory but possibly true
hook: PARADOX: two contradictory things that are both true.
story: Paradoxical. Ishrat's doctor told her something strange: to cure her constant tiredness, she should exercise more. How could spending energy give her more energy? Yet after a month of morning walks, she felt less tired than ever. The advice was paradoxical: seemingly contradictory, but possibly true. A paradox looks impossible but holds a truth, like less is more. Para means against, and dox means opinion, as in orthodox: a paradox goes against expectation. Synonyms: contradictory, counterintuitive.

gre.s: It may seem ____ that adding new roads can worsen traffic, yet studies show that extra lanes often attract so many new drivers that congestion increases.
gre.clue: yet studies show

en: Continued effort despite difficulty or delay
hook: PER-SEVERE-ANCE: persisting through SEVERE difficulty.
story: Perseverance. Hasan failed the civil service exam on his first attempt. He studied for another year and failed again, by only a few marks. His friends gave up and took other jobs. Hasan sat for it a third time, and this time he passed. Today he is an officer in Rangpur. He succeeded through perseverance: continued effort despite difficulty or delay. The verb is persevere. Think: per means through, so you push through severe times. Synonyms: persistence, tenacity, doggedness.

gre.s: The team's eventual success owed less to brilliance than to sheer ____: they repeated the failed experiment hundreds of times before obtaining a usable result.
gre.clue: they repeated the failed experiment hundreds of times

en: To cause to become; to provide or give
hook: RENDER: RENDERS it into a new state.
story: Render. The night before her thesis was due, a power surge fried Moushumi's laptop and rendered it useless. Her friend Tanha arrived at midnight with her own computer and rendered all the help she could, retyping chapters until dawn. To render is to cause to become, as in rendered useless or rendered speechless. It also means to provide or give: to render a service, to render aid. A court renders a verdict, and a singer renders a song. Synonyms: make, provide, deliver.

gre.s: Throughout the crisis, volunteers continued to ____ assistance to stranded travelers, offering food, shelter, and free rides to the nearest town.
gre.clue: offering food, shelter, and free rides to the nearest town

en: The complete set of skills, songs, or works someone can perform
hook: REPERTOIRE: the REPORT of everything you can perform.
story: Repertoire. Uncle Kader plays harmonium at every family wedding. He knows Tagore songs, Nazrul songs, Lalon songs, old film hits, and even a few English tunes. Whatever the guests request, he can play it. His repertoire is enormous: the complete set of songs, skills, or works someone can perform. The word is French; repertory theatre companies keep a repertoire of plays. A chess player has a repertoire of openings, and a teacher a repertoire of tricks. Synonyms: range, stock, arsenal.

gre.s: Although the pianist was celebrated mainly for her Chopin, her ____ was surprisingly broad, extending from medieval dances to experimental contemporary works.
gre.clue: extending from medieval dances to experimental contemporary works

en: Able to recover quickly from difficulties
hook: RESILIENT: RE-SPRINGS back like a spring.
story: Resilient. Every few years, a cyclone flattens parts of the Bangladeshi coast. Yet within weeks, families rebuild their homes, replant rice, and reopen their tea stalls, sometimes stronger than before. People who study disasters often call these communities resilient: able to recover quickly from difficulties. Resilient comes from Latin for leaping back; think of a rubber ball that bounces back after being squashed. Resilient materials return to shape; resilient people return to life. Synonyms: tough, hardy, buoyant. Opposite: fragile.

gre.s: The economy proved surprisingly ____: although the crisis wiped out a fifth of its output, it regained its former strength in less than two years.
gre.clue: it regained its former strength in less than two years

en: Firmly determined; unwavering
hook: RESOLUTE: full of RESOLVE.
story: Resolute. Tahmina's family wanted her to marry at seventeen. She refused, calmly but firmly, again and again, for two years. She studied through the arguments, took tuition jobs to pay her own fees, and won a place at university. Nothing could change her mind. She was resolute: firmly determined, unwavering. Resolute comes from resolve, a firm decision. A resolute leader does not bend under pressure. Synonyms: determined, steadfast, unwavering, unyielding. Opposites: irresolute, vacillating.

gre.s: Despite years of threats and imprisonment, the activist remained ____ in her demands for reform, refusing every offer of compromise from the government.
gre.clue: refusing every offer of compromise from the government

en: Bending and moving easily; flexible
hook: SUPPLE: as soft and flexible as SUPPLE leather.
story: Supple. Shathi has practised classical dance since she was five. She can bend backward until her palms touch the floor and twist her wrists into shapes that make audiences gasp. Her body is supple: bending and moving easily, flexible. Good leather is supple, soft and pliable. A supple mind adapts quickly to new ideas. Say supple aloud, and it even sounds soft and springy. Synonyms: flexible, pliant, lithe, limber. Opposites: stiff, rigid.

gre.s: Years of daily yoga had kept the old man remarkably ____: at eighty, he could still bend easily enough to touch his toes.
gre.clue: he could still bend easily enough to touch his toes

en: Great courage in the face of danger, especially in battle
hook: VALOR: VALUE of a hero's courage.
story: Valor. On the twenty-first of February 1952, students in Dhaka marched for the right to speak Bangla, though gatherings had been banned and police stood ready. Some were shot and killed. Every year, the nation lays flowers at the Shaheed Minar to honour their valor: great courage in the face of danger. Valor is used especially for bravery in battle; soldiers receive medals for valor. The adjective is valiant. Synonyms: bravery, heroism, gallantry. Opposite: cowardice.

gre.s: The soldier was decorated for his ____, having repeatedly crossed enemy lines under heavy fire to carry wounded comrades to safety.
gre.clue: having repeatedly crossed enemy lines under heavy fire
